lessons.title: Marking Fractions on a Number Line

activities.prompt: How can you show fractions on a number line?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Fractions on a Number Line
activities.body:
Imagine you meet a number line that can show lengths equal to whole units. You can also use it to mark lengths equal to fractions.

Start by looking from 0 to 1. This distance is one unit long. You split it into two equal parts. Each part is one half.

In the first example, the blue line is one half unit long. You mark that point carefully. This helps you see where one half belongs.

Now explore other divisions. You can divide one unit into three equal parts. You can also divide it into five equal parts. Each equal part marks another fraction.

What happens with finer sharing? You can divide one unit into eight equal parts. Between 0 and 1, there are uncountably many fractions. The number line keeps offering more places to explore.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Fractions on a Number Line
activities.body: A number line shows lengths from 0 to 1. The gap between them is one whole unit. You can divide this gap into equal parts. Two equal parts make halves. You can also divide one unit into three, five or eight equal parts. Marking these parts helps you place fractions between 0 and 1.
keyPoints: The distance from 0 to 1 is one whole unit.
One unit can be divided into equal parts.
Equal parts show fraction lengths.
activities.explanation: This helps you see how fractions fit between 0 and 1.

activities.prompt: A one-unit length is divided into 5 equal parts. How many equal parts make up the one-unit length?

steps: Use 0 to 1 because that distance is one whole unit.
Divide it into two equal parts because each part is one half.
Mark that part's end because it is one half unit from 0.
So the marked point shows one half of the whole unit.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.title: Many Fraction Lengths
activities.body: One unit can also be split into three equal parts. It can also be split into five or eight equal parts. Each marked part shows a fraction length. There are endless (never ending) fractions between 0 and 1. All of them fit on the same number line.
keyPoints: Equal parts can show different fraction lengths.
Many fraction lengths fit between 0 and 1.
A number line can mark fraction lengths.
activities.explanation: Equal parts can show many fractions between 0 and 1.

activities.explanation: Good choice! The number line can show lengths equal to fractions as well as whole units.

Therefore, 5 equal parts are shaded.
activities.hint: The numerator tells how many equal parts are shaded.

activities.prompt: How do you compare a fraction with one whole?

activities.title: A Tour of Mixed Numbers
activities.body:
Imagine meeting fractions during this tour. You may wonder how each compares with one whole unit. If the numerator is smaller than the denominator, the fraction is smaller than one unit. If the numerator is larger than the denominator, the fraction is greater than one unit.

You try three halves, five halves and seven halves. All three are greater than one unit. Now look again at three halves. It equals one whole unit plus one half. Next, you meet four thirds. This fraction is also greater than one unit. Some fractions greater than one cannot be written as mixed numbers.

You now discover a mixed number. It contains a whole-number part. The fraction smaller than one in it is called the fractional part. You next meet eight thirds. It is also called two and two thirds.

Before you finish, write a mixed number as a regular fraction. You can check each fraction by comparing its numerator with its denominator. Smaller numerators show fractions smaller than one unit. Larger numerators show fractions greater than one unit.

Eight thirds is also called two and two thirds.

activities.title: Equivalent Fractions and Lowest Terms
activities.body:
Imagine two strips of equal length. One is split in half. The other is split into quarters. You hold one half and two quarters. Do they cover the same length?

They cover the same length. Different fractional units can show equal shares. Fractions with equal shares are called equivalent fractions. Three sixths also match one half. So, one half, two quarters and three sixths are equivalent.

Now picture sharing units among children. When the same units are shared among more children, each child’s share is less. When the same number of children share more units, each child gets a larger share.

Sometimes an equivalent fraction is not in its simplest form. Six ninths has the simpler form two thirds. In lowest terms, a fraction’s numerator and denominator have no common factor except 1. In lowest terms, they are as small as possible.

To find lowest terms, divide the numerator and denominator by their highest common factor. You can also multiply both by the same number and keep equivalent fractions equal. For example, thirty-six sixtieths becomes three fifths in lowest terms.

lessons.title: Comparing, Adding and Subtracting Fractions

activities.prompt: How can you compare and combine fractional pieces fairly?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Fractional Journey
activities.body:
Imagine meeting fractional pieces on a maths journey. Which is larger? How can you join or break them apart?

First, change the fractions to equivalent fractions with the same denominator. Then compare their numerators. Forty-five is a common multiple of five and nine. You can use it as a shared denominator.

Now suppose you add fractions with the same fractional unit. You add their fractional units. If the fractional units differ, first change them to equivalent fractions with the same denominator. Then add the numerators and keep the denominator. Write the result in lowest terms when needed.

Subtraction follows a similar path. First, change fractions to equivalent fractions with the same fractional unit. Then subtract the numerators and keep the same denominator.

Words from India give us a glimpse of fractions. In Sanskrit, a fraction was called bhinna, meaning broken. Bhaga and an sha were names for a part or piece. General fractions and their arithmetic rules were first introduced in India.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: A Helpful Fraction Plan
activities.body: To compare fractions, first use equivalent fractions. Make the denominators the same. Then compare the numerators. To add fractions, make the fractional units the same. Add the numerators. Keep the denominator. To subtract fractions, use the same denominator. Then subtract the numerators. Write the answer in lowest terms when needed. In Sanskrit, a fraction was called bhinna. It means broken. Bhaga and an sha meant a part or piece.
keyPoints: Compare fractions using equivalent fractions with the same denominator.
Add or subtract the numerators when the units match.
Bhaga and an sha meant a part or piece.
activities.explanation: These steps help you compare, add and subtract fractions.

activities.prompt: Compare 5/10 and 3/10. How many parts out of 10 are in the larger fraction?
steps: Both fractions have denominator 10, so their fractional units are already the same.
Compare the numerators 5 and 3; the larger numerator gives the larger fraction.
The larger fraction has 5 parts out of 10.

gen.template: Compare {a}/{d} and {c}/{d}. How many parts out of {d} are in the larger fraction?
steps: Both fractions have denominator {d}, so their fractional units are already the same.
Compare the numerators {a} and {c}; the larger numerator gives the larger fraction.
The larger fraction has {answer} parts out of {d}.
gen.hint: Notice that both fractions already have the same denominator.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.title: Which Fraction Is Greater?
activities.prompt: Which fraction is greater: 9/5 or 5/9?
options: They are equal
You cannot tell
activities.explanation: With denominator 45, compare numerators 81 and 25. Since 81 is greater, 9/5 is greater.

activities.prompt: When two fractions have the same denominator, compare their numerators.
activities.explanation: Now the fractions have one denominator. So compare their numerators.

activities.prompt: Compare 2/5 and 2/9. How many forty-fifths are in the larger fraction?
activities.explanation: Forty-five is a common multiple of five and nine, so use it as the common denominator. The first fraction becomes 18 forty-fifths, and the second becomes 10 forty-fifths. Compare 18 and 10; the larger numerator gives the larger fraction. The larger fraction contains 18 forty-fifths.
steps: Forty-five is a common multiple of five and nine, so use it as the common denominator.
The first fraction becomes 18 forty-fifths, and the second becomes 10 forty-fifths.
Compare 18 and 10; the larger numerator gives the larger fraction.
The larger fraction contains 18 forty-fifths.
activities.hint: First write both fractions with denominator forty-five.

gen.template: Compare {a}/5 and {b}/9. How many forty-fifths are in the larger fraction?
steps: Forty-five is a common multiple of five and nine, so use it as the common denominator.
The first fraction becomes {r45} forty-fifths, and the second becomes {m45} forty-fifths.
Compare {r45} and {m45}; the larger numerator gives the larger fraction.
The larger fraction contains {answer} forty-fifths.
gen.hint: First write both fractions with denominator forty-five.

activities.title: Match the Fraction Job
activities.prompt: Match each fraction job with the correct step.
pairs: Make the fractional units the same
Add numerators and keep the denominator
Subtract numerators and keep the same denominator
activities.explanation: Matching fractional units comes first. Then compare, add or subtract the numerators.

activities.title: Order the Addition Steps
activities.prompt: Put the addition steps in the correct order.
items: Change to equivalent fractions with the same denominator
Write the result in lowest terms if needed
activities.explanation: Make the fractional units equal before adding the numerators.

activities.prompt: Each of two equal-sized boxes holds 12 marbles; one box is 5/12 full and the other is 4/12 full. How many marbles are in the fuller box?
activities.explanation: The two boxes have the same denominator 12, so their fractional units are the same. Compare the numerators 5 and 4; the larger one shows the fuller box. The fuller box contains 5 marbles.
steps: The two boxes have the same denominator 12, so their fractional units are the same.
Compare the numerators 5 and 4; the larger one shows the fuller box.
The fuller box contains 5 marbles.
activities.hint: Both boxes have the same fractional unit, so compare their numerators.

activities.prompt: Both cricket teams scored 45 runs in all. Ravi scored 2/5 of his team's runs and Meena scored 3/9 of her team's runs. How many runs is the larger score?
activities.explanation: Forty-five is a common multiple of five and nine, so use it as the common denominator. Ravi's score becomes 18 runs, and Meena's score becomes 15 runs. Compare 18 and 15; the larger numerator gives the larger score. The larger score is 18 runs.
steps: Forty-five is a common multiple of five and nine, so use it as the common denominator.
Ravi's score becomes 18 runs, and Meena's score becomes 15 runs.

The larger score is 18 runs.

activities.context: One roti is shared equally between two children, and each child gets half a roti. Another roti is shared equally among four children, so each child gets one quarter. A further roti is shared equally among five children, and each child gets one fifth. The children compare the shares from the two-child, four-child, and five-child groups.
activities.prompt: If the five-child group were instead asked to share one roti equally among nine children, what would each child get?
options: Half of the roti
One quarter of the roti
One fifth of the roti
One ninth of the roti

why.Half of the roti: Half is the share when one roti is shared between two children.
why.One quarter of the roti: One quarter is the share when one roti is shared among four children.
why.One fifth of the roti: One fifth applies only when five children share the roti.

activities.explanation: Nine equal parts make each child's share one ninth.

activities.context: One roti is shared equally between two children, and each child gets half a roti. Another roti is shared equally among four children, so each child gets one quarter. A further roti is shared equally among five children, and each child gets one fifth. The children compare the shares from the two-child, four-child, and five-child groups.
activities.prompt: If one child leaves the five-child group and the remaining children keep sharing the same roti equally, how does each remaining child's share change?
options: It becomes larger than one fifth.
It becomes smaller than one fifth.
It stays exactly one fifth.
It becomes one half of the roti.

Removing a child does not make the equal shares smaller.
The share stays one fifth only if five children continue sharing.
Half is the share for two children, not four children.

activities.explanation: Four children remain, so each receives one quarter of the roti.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between one half and one quarter.
activities.answer: One half is the equal share when one roti is shared between two children. One quarter is the equal share when one roti is shared among four children. Since sharing with more people gives each person less, one quarter is smaller than one half, although both are fractional units.
points: Half is the share for two children.
Quarter is the share for four children.
More children sharing means less for each child.
Half is larger than quarter.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a mathematics activity, a student examines chikki and a paper strip. The bigger chikki piece contains three one-quarter pieces. Another chikki is broken into three equal pieces, making one-third pieces. Six equal parts of a whole chikki can have different shapes. The student treats the strip as one unit long, folds it into two equal parts, then folds the already-folded strip again. The activity uses fractional units to describe and measure quantities.
activities.prompt: After the student folds the strip once and then folds the already-folded strip again, what is true about the strip?
options: The strip has four equal parts.
The strip has three equal parts.
The strip has six equal parts.
The strip still has only two equal parts.

Three equal parts occur in the chikki example, not the folded strip.
Six equal parts belong to a different activity with the whole chikki.
why.The strip still has only two equal parts: Two equal parts describe the strip after only the first fold.

activities.explanation: Folding the two parts again produces four equal parts in total.

activities.context: During a mathematics activity, a student examines chikki and a paper strip. The bigger chikki piece contains three one-quarter pieces. Another chikki is broken into three equal pieces, making one-third pieces. Six equal parts of a whole chikki can have different shapes. The student treats the strip as one unit long, folds it into two equal parts, then folds the already-folded strip again. The activity uses fractional units to describe and measure quantities.
activities.prompt: If the student collects the three one-quarter pieces from the bigger chikki piece, which description should be written?
options: Three quarters
Three thirds
One quarter
One third

why.Three thirds: Each collected unit is a quarter, not a third.
why.One quarter: Only one of the three units has been counted.
why.One third: One third is the size of each piece when a chikki has three equal parts.

activities.explanation: Collecting three one-quarter units gives a total of three quarters.

activities.context: During a mathematics activity, a student examines chikki and a paper strip. The bigger chikki piece contains three one-quarter pieces. Another chikki is broken into three equal pieces, making one-third pieces. Six equal parts of a whole chikki can have different shapes. The student treats the strip as one unit long, folds it into two equal parts, then folds the already-folded strip again. The activity uses fractional units to describe and measure quantities.
activities.prompt: If the student divides a whole chikki into six equal parts and arranges them with different shapes, what should the student conclude?
options: The parts remain equal even when their shapes differ.
The changed shapes make some parts larger than others.
The six parts are one-third pieces.
The six parts together make one quarter of the whole.

why.The changed shapes make some parts large: Changing a part's shape does not change the original equal division.
One-third pieces result from dividing the whole into three equal pieces.
why.The six parts together make one quarter: The six parts together make the whole, not one quarter of it.

activities.explanation: Equal parts can have different shapes without losing their equal size.

activities.prompt: Explain how folding the paper strip produces fractional units and what parts result after the two folds.
activities.answer: The strip begins as one unit long. Folding it into two equal parts creates two half-unit parts. When the already-folded strip is folded again, it creates four equal parts. These fractional units can be used to measure and describe quantities.
points: The original strip is one unit long.
The first fold makes two half-unit parts.
The second fold makes four equal parts.
Fractional units describe and measure quantities.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A tailor needs to place several marks on a ribbon. The tailor first marks 0 and 1, showing that the distance between them is one unit. The distance is then divided into two equal parts, and a blue line shows one half unit. Next, the tailor uses three equal parts, then five equal parts, and finally eight equal parts on the same distance. The tailor is also told that uncountably many fractions lie between the end marks.
activities.prompt: Why does the blue line show one half unit?
options: Each chosen piece has half the length of the whole interval.
Each chosen piece has one third of the interval's length.
Each chosen piece has one fifth of the interval's length.
Each chosen piece has one eighth of the interval's length.

why.Each chosen piece has one third of the i: One third would require three equal pieces.
why.Each chosen piece has one fifth of the i: One fifth would require five equal pieces.
why.Each chosen piece has one eighth of the: One eighth would require eight equal pieces.

activities.explanation: The interval was split into two equal pieces.

activities.context: A tailor needs to place several marks on a ribbon. The tailor first marks 0 and 1, showing that the distance between them is one unit. The distance is then divided into two equal parts, and a blue line shows one half unit. Next, the tailor uses three equal parts, then five equal parts, and finally eight equal parts on the same distance. The tailor is also told that uncountably many fractions lie between the end marks.
activities.prompt: If the tailor changes the five equal parts to eight equal parts, what remains true?
options: The same interval would be split into eight equal-length sections.
The same interval would be split into five equal-length sections.
The same interval would be split into three equal-length sections.
The same interval would be split into two equal-length sections.

why.The same interval would be split into fi: Five equal parts would mean the change was not made.
why.The same interval would be split into th: Three equal parts would mean the unit was divided differently.
why.The same interval would be split into tw: Two equal parts would show halves rather than eighths.

activities.explanation: Eight equal parts are still marked within the interval from 0 to 1.

activities.prompt: How does marking one half differ from marking one third on a number line?
activities.answer: One half is marked by dividing the distance from 0 to 1 into two equal parts and marking one part. One third is marked by dividing the same distance into three equal parts and marking one part. Thus, the one-third mark is closer to 0 than the one-half mark.
points: The distance from 0 to 1 is one unit.
One half uses two equal parts.
One third uses three equal parts.
The one-third mark is closer to 0.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school fair, a juice stall records how much drink it pours. One small order needs four thirds of a jug, while one large order needs seven halves of a jug. The stall worker writes one amount as a mixed number and leaves the other as a regular fraction, because not every fraction greater than one unit can be written as a mixed number. Each amount is greater than one unit.
activities.prompt: If the small order changes from four thirds of a jug to three halves of a jug, what should the worker tell the customer?
options: The new amount is greater than one unit and equals one whole unit plus one half.
The new amount is a fraction smaller than one unit.
The new amount no longer has a whole-number part.
The new amount is less than one whole unit plus one half.

why.The new amount is a fraction smaller tha: A fraction smaller than one has its numerator smaller than its denominator.
why.The new amount no longer has a whole-num: Three halves can be shown with a whole-number part.
why.The new amount is less than one whole un: Three halves equals one whole unit plus one half, not less.

activities.explanation: The numerator three is larger than the denominator two.

activities.context: At a school fair, a juice stall records how much drink it pours. One small order needs four thirds of a jug, while one large order needs seven halves of a jug. The stall worker writes one amount as a mixed number and leaves the other as a regular fraction, because not every fraction greater than one unit can be written as a mixed number. Each amount is greater than one unit.
activities.prompt: If the worker changes the regular-fraction entry to a fraction whose numerator is smaller than its denominator, what would happen?
options: It would be a fraction smaller than one unit.
It would be a fraction greater than one unit.
It would become a mixed number with a whole-number part.
It would still equal the original greater-than-one amount.

why.It would be a fraction greater than one: A fraction above one unit has the opposite numerator and denominator sizes.
why.It would become a mixed number with a wh: A smaller fraction does not become a mixed number by this change.
why.It would still equal the original greate: The changed fraction would no longer be greater than one unit.

activities.explanation: A numerator smaller than the denominator identifies a fraction below one unit.

activities.prompt: Explain why three halves is greater than one unit and how it can be shown as a mixed number.
activities.answer: Three halves is greater than one unit because its numerator, three, is larger than its denominator, two. It is also equal to one whole unit plus one half. In that form, the whole-number part shows one whole unit, and the fractional part shows the remaining half.
points: Names the numerator and denominator.
Explains that three is larger than two.
Shows one whole unit plus one half.
Identifies the whole-number and fractional parts.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: How does sharing the same squares among more children compare with giving more squares to the same number of children?
activities.answer: When the same squares are shared among more children, each child receives less. If the same number of children receive more squares, each child gets a larger share. Therefore, changing the number of children or the number of squares changes the size of each child’s share.
points: Explains that more children sharing the same squares means a smaller share each.
Explains that more squares shared by the same children means a larger share each.
Clearly contrasts the two changes.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a recycling centre, a student sorts two piles of material that look equal in size. The first pile is measured in fifths, while the second is measured in ninths. Before deciding which pile is larger, the student finds that forty-five works for both measurements. The student rewrites them as equivalent fractions with denominator forty-five. Looking at the numerators, the student selects the pile represented by the greater numerator.
activities.prompt: After both piles are written with denominator forty-five, how should the student decide which pile is larger?
options: Choose the equivalent fraction with the larger numerator.
Choose the equivalent fraction with the smaller numerator.
Choose the pile whose original fractional unit has the larger denominator.
Choose the pile written in ninths regardless of its numerator.

why.Choose the equivalent fraction with the: Reversing the comparison rule gives the wrong choice.
why.Choose the pile whose original fractiona: The original denominator alone does not decide the comparison.
why.Choose the pile written in ninths regard: The number of fractional parts alone does not decide the comparison.

activities.explanation: With a shared denominator, the larger numerator represents the larger fraction.

activities.context: At a recycling centre, a student sorts two piles of material that look equal in size. The first pile is measured in fifths, while the second is measured in ninths. Before deciding which pile is larger, the student finds that forty-five works for both measurements. The student rewrites them as equivalent fractions with denominator forty-five. Looking at the numerators, the student selects the pile represented by the greater numerator.
activities.prompt: If the student must add a fifth-sized portion and a ninth-sized portion, what should the student do next?
options: Change them to equivalent fractions with the same denominator, add the numerators, and keep the denominator.
Change them to equivalent fractions with the same denominator, subtract the numerators, and keep the denominator.
Add the denominators and keep the original numerators.
Compare the numerators after using different denominators.

why.Change them to equivalent fractions with: Subtracting the numerators would find a difference rather than a sum.
why.Add the denominators and keep the origin: Adding the denominators does not follow the fraction addition rule.
why.Compare the numerators after using diffe: Different denominators must first be changed to the same denominator.

activities.explanation: This follows the rule for adding fractions with different fractional units.

activities.prompt: Explain how the student should compare fractions with denominators five and nine and decide which is larger.
activities.answer: First, change both fractions to equivalent fractions with denominator forty-five, because forty-five is a common multiple of five and nine. Next, compare the numerators of the equivalent fractions. The fraction with the larger numerator is the larger fraction.
points: Uses forty-five as the shared denominator.
Changes both fractions to equivalent fractions.
Compares the numerators.
Chooses the fraction with the larger numerator.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

pairs: one whole unit plus one half
activities.explanation: Three halves is one whole unit plus one half. Eight thirds is also called two and two thirds.

items: Change to equivalent fractions with the same denominator.

chapters.title: Playing with Constructions
chapters.summary: In this chapter: artwork with a compass; squares and rectangles; constructing squares and rectangles; exploring rectangles.

lessons.title: Artwork with a Compass

activities.prompt: What wonders can your compass uncover on a page?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your Compass Adventure
activities.body:
You open a book of artwork. It includes straight lines, circles, and other figures among curves. Your compass feels like a tiny guide. Soon, you meet a point called P.

From P, mark as many points as possible in different directions. Each point is 4 cm from P. All such points form a circle. P is called the centre.

The compass tip and pencil point must be 4 cm apart. Keep the compass point fixed and move only the pencil. The curve it makes is a circle. The distance from the centre to any point on the circle is the radius.

The chapter asks whether using instruments makes construction easier. You can explore this while drawing. The length of the central line is not specified. So, focus on your compass.

In Wavy Wave, you begin with a surprise. The first wave is drawn as a half circle. Hold the compass steady and let the pencil travel. Soon, straight edges and flowing curves share your page.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How a Compass Makes a Circle
activities.body: A compass can draw a circle. Set its two points 4 cm apart. Keep the compass point fixed. Move only the pencil. Every point on the new circle is 4 cm from P. P is the centre. The radius is the distance from the centre to any point on the circle. Do tools make drawing easier? The chapter asks this.
keyPoints: Keep the compass point fixed and move only the pencil.
Every point on the circle is 4 cm from P.
P is the centre, and the radius reaches from P to the circle.
activities.explanation: Keeping the compass point still keeps every circle point the same distance from P.

activities.prompt: Place the compass tip at P and set the pencil point 6 cm away. What is the radius of the circle in cm?
steps: Keep the compass tip fixed at P and set the pencil point 6 cm away.
P is the centre, so the radius is the distance from P to the circle.
6 cm = 6 cm, so the radius is 6 cm.

gen.template: Place the compass tip at P and set the pencil point {opening} cm away. What is the radius of the circle in cm?
steps: Keep the compass tip fixed at P and set the pencil point {opening} cm away.
P is the centre, so the radius is the distance from P to the circle.
{opening} cm = {answer} cm, so the radius is {answer} cm.
gen.hint: Set the compass at the distance stated in the question.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: How can I draw around P with every dot 4 cm away?
steps: Use a 4 cm opening because it fixes the circle's radius.
Place the tip at P because P will be the circle's centre.
Keep the tip fixed so only the pencil moves around P.
All its points stay 4 cm from P, making a circle.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.title: The Compass Shape
activities.prompt: Which shape does the curve made by a compass make?
options: A straight line
A circle
A half circle
A central line
activities.explanation: The curve made by the compass is a circle.

activities.prompt: Mark points in different directions from P, with every point 2 cm from P. What is the distance from P to any one marked point, in cm?
activities.explanation: Each marked point is 2 cm from P. All the marked points in different directions have the same distance from P. Therefore, the distance to any one point is 2 cm.
steps: Each marked point is 2 cm from P.
All the marked points in different directions have the same distance from P.
Therefore, the distance to any one point is 2 cm.
activities.hint: Use the distance from P to one of the marked points.

gen.template: Mark points in different directions from P, with every point {r} cm from P. What is the distance from P to any one marked point, in cm?
steps: Each marked point is {r} cm from P.
All the marked points in different directions have the same distance from P.
Therefore, the distance to any one point is {answer} cm.
gen.hint: Use the distance from P to one of the marked points.

activities.prompt: Draw two circles with the same centre P, using compass openings 2 cm and 6 cm. How many cm farther from P is a point on the second circle than a point on the first circle?
activities.explanation: Both circles have centre P, so their openings are their radii. The first radius is 2 cm and the second radius is 6 cm. Their difference is 4 cm, so the answer is 4 cm.
steps: Both circles have centre P, so their openings are their radii.
The first radius is 2 cm and the second radius is 6 cm.
Their difference is 4 cm, so the answer is 4 cm.
activities.hint: Identify which circle reaches farther from P.

gen.template: Draw two circles with the same centre P, using compass openings {a} cm and {b} cm. How many cm farther from P is a point on the second circle than a point on the first circle?
steps: Both circles have centre P, so their openings are their radii.
The first radius is {a} cm and the second radius is {b} cm.
Their difference is {difference} cm, so the answer is {answer} cm.
gen.hint: Identify which circle reaches farther from P.

activities.prompt: Mark 4 points in different directions from P, each 3 cm away. What is the total distance from P to all the marked points, in cm?
activities.explanation: Each of the 4 points is 3 cm from P. Multiply the number of points by the distance of each point from P. 4 x 3 = 12 cm, so the total distance is 12 cm.
steps: Each of the 4 points is 3 cm from P.
Multiply the number of points by the distance of each point from P.
4 x 3 = 12 cm, so the total distance is 12 cm.
activities.hint: First find the distance from P to one marked point.

steps: Each of the {n} points is {r} cm from P.
Multiply the number of points by the distance of each point from P.
{n} x {r} = {total} cm, so the total distance is {answer} cm.
gen.hint: First find the distance from P to one marked point.

activities.title: Points Around P
activities.prompt: Why are all the points 4 cm from P on one circle?
options: They all have the same distance from P.
They all lie on one straight line.
They all have different distances from P.
Their middle line has a fixed length.
activities.explanation: All these points are 4 cm from P. So they make one circle.

activities.title: Circle Words
activities.prompt: Match each word or phrase with its correct partner.
pairs: distance from the centre to the circle
activities.explanation: P is the centre, while the radius reaches from the centre to the circle.

activities.title: Draw a Circle
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Set the compass tip and pencil 4 cm apart.
activities.explanation: Set the gap, hold one point, move the pencil, and watch the circle appear.

activities.prompt: At a market stall, a round laddoo tray is drawn as a circle with centre P and compass opening 7 cm. How many cm is the distance from P to any point on its circular edge?
activities.explanation: The compass tip is at P, so P is the centre of the tray's circle. The pencil point is 7 cm from the compass tip. The distance from the centre to the circular edge is 7 cm.
steps: The compass tip is at P, so P is the centre of the tray's circle.

activities.title: A Shape Tour
activities.body:
You begin with two familiar shapes. Each has straight sides.

First, you meet a rectangle. Its corners are A, B, C and D. The sides travel around it as AB, BC, CD and DA. The angles at its corners are ∠A, ∠B, ∠C and ∠D. Each one measures 90°.

Notice that AD and BC make another pair of opposite sides. These sides have equal lengths. Now, you turn the rectangle. It remains a rectangle.

Next, you find a square. All its sides have equal lengths. Its angles still measure 90°. Turn it carefully. Its side lengths and angles do not change. Even when the square is turned, each angle remains 90°.

Finally, you learn a naming trick. A valid name travels around the rectangle. You can start at any corner. Then follow the sides in order. Try A, B, C, D, A, or begin somewhere else.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

Every rectangle angle measures 90°.
A square has equal sides and 90° angles.

activities.title: Squares and Rectangles
activities.body:
First, you construct square PQRS, with each side measuring 6 cm. Draw a perpendicular to PQ through P. Mark point S on the perpendicular. Set PS at 6 cm using a ruler. You can also mark S using a compass.

Now draw a perpendicular to PQ through Q. Using the compass lets you mark the next point easily. With care, you build the square PQRS. Each side has the same length of 6 cm.

Next, you construct a rectangle with sides 4 cm and 6 cm. Draw its first side with your ruler. Use the compass to mark the next point. Check the finished rectangle against both rectangle properties.

You also construct a rectangle with sides 2 cm and 10 cm. Repeat the careful construction steps. Use the ruler to set the lengths. Then use the compass to mark each next point.

Finally, notice the chapter’s special question. It asks about a four-sided figure with all angles equal to 90º. Which properties will you check first?

activities.prompt: Could two points hide a surprising distance?

activities.title: A Rectangle Tour
activities.body:
Imagine you begin inside a rectangle. Point X can move anywhere along the side AD. You may place X at either end point, A or D.

Point Y can be placed at either end point, B or C. You can find distance XY by measuring line XY. Now you can compare different placements.

When X and Y are equally placed, XY equals AB. Next, you choose placements that lie farthest apart. The farthest distance between X and Y equals AC or BD.

Now shift your attention to squares. You can divide the rectangle into two identical squares. All the shorter lines in that rectangle are equal.

You can also divide the rectangle into three identical squares. For three identical squares, the length is three times the breadth. Measure again, and explore every placement.

activities.title: Points and distances in a rectangle
activities.body: Point X can move along AD. Point Y can be placed at B or C. Distance XY is found by measuring line XY. When X and Y are equally placed, XY equals AB. The farthest distance equals AC or BD. A rectangle can split into two identical squares. It can split into three identical squares. With three squares, length is three times breadth. Breadth means the shorter side.

Three identical squares make length three times breadth.

lessons.title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares

activities.prompt: What do diagonals reveal about the corners of a rectangle?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Rectangle Diagonals
activities.body:
You begin with rectangle PQRS. The lines PR and QS are called the diagonals. You follow each one across the shape. You wonder how these crossing lines affect the corners.

At P and R, you find right angles. These are opposite angles. At Q and S, you find the other opposite pair. A diagonal divides each pair into smaller angles. The diagonal PR divides angle R into two smaller angles. It also divides angle P into the angles c and d.

When both diagonals meet, they form eight angles. You count them around the crossing point. Each diagonal splits the opposite corners into smaller angles. You compare the pairs as you trace them.

Your exploration also includes a rectangle with all four sides equal. When two adjacent sides are equal, the rectangle becomes a square. To find D, you draw a perpendicular to BC at C. A compass can mark D so that AD equals BC. Your tour ends with a square.

lessons.title: Points Equidistant from Two Given Points

activities.prompt: Find a point that is equidistant (the same distance) from two places. How can circles help?

activities.title: Finding the Equidistant Point
activities.body:
Every border line of the house has length 5 cm. The task is to find point A, 5 cm from both B and C. Start by trying to find this point with a ruler. This method needs trial and error. You test possible points and check both distances.

Now you simplify the construction by using a compass. Draw a circle centred at B, with a radius of 5 cm. All points on this circle are the same distance from its centre. So every point on it is 5 cm from B. The correct point A can be found on this circle.

Next, draw a circle centred at C, with a radius of 5 cm. Look where the two circles meet. Their intersection gives the point A. Only parts of the two circles are needed to find A.

Join A to B and A to C using straight lines. These are the lines AB and AC. Then draw an arc centred at A. Choose the arc so that it touches B and C. You have now completed the construction.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: seeing symmetry in patterns; lines of symmetry; reflection and making symmetrical shapes; rotational symmetry.

lessons.title: Seeing Symmetry in Patterns

activities.prompt: What might make a colourful pattern look special when you turn it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Patterns in Sight
activities.body:
You meet a flower. Look at it from many different angles. The flower looks the same from many different angles.

Now a butterfly appears, showing very attractive colours. Notice how repeated parts of a figure can follow a definite pattern. You compare each shape before deciding what matches.

Next, you see red petals in a rangoli. Turn the picture and watch those petals. They come back onto themselves after a turn. The petals return when you rotate the rangoli by 90˚ around its centre. The other parts return in the same way.

After that, you meet a pinwheel. Start with its hexagon. You can spot the repeating pattern by looking there first. Then your eyes follow the repeated parts around the pinwheel.

Finally, you look at a set of pictures. The first four pictures are symmetrical, but the last one is not. You also meet a cloud picture. It is not symmetrical. The clouds have no repetitive pattern. You now know that symmetry means parts of a figure repeat in a definite pattern.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What Is Symmetry?
activities.body: Symmetry means that parts of a figure repeat in a definite pattern. The flower looks the same from many angles. The rangoli's red petals return after a turn. Its other parts return too. A pinwheel's repeating pattern can be spotted by looking at its hexagon. The first four pictures are symmetrical, but the last one is not.
keyPoints: Symmetry means parts repeat in a definite pattern.
The rangoli's petals return after a turn.
A pinwheel's hexagon helps reveal its pattern.
activities.explanation: Look for parts that return in the same way.

The whole pattern has 12 petals.

gen.hint: Multiply the number of rows by the number of petals in one row.

The rangoli is therefore symmetrical because its parts repeat in a definite pattern.

activities.title: Turning a Picture
activities.body: A turn can reveal symmetry. When the rangoli turns by 90˚ around its centre, its red petals return. The other parts return in the same way. Symmetry is not present in every picture. The cloud picture is not symmetrical. Its clouds also have no repetitive pattern.

The other parts return in the same way.
The cloud picture is not symmetrical.

activities.title: The Perfect Folding Tour
activities.body:
Imagine you meet a blue triangle with a dotted line. You imagine folding along the dotted line. You lift one side and place it over the other. One half covers the other half completely.

That perfect covering tells you the fold works. Two matching halves are called mirror halves. The folding line is called a line of symmetry. Now you know what to look for during this tour.

Next, you find a square and imagine different folds. A vertical fold gives a line of symmetry in a square. A horizontal fold also gives you one. A diagonal fold gives another line of symmetry in the square.

Try the two puzzle-piece halves as you continue. These two puzzle-piece halves are not mirror halves. They fail the perfect-overlap test. So their folding line cannot be a line of symmetry.

Finally, you notice that one shape can offer several perfect folds. A figure can have more than one line of symmetry. The square guides you through this idea. Your turn is to hunt for lines that make matching halves.

activities.title: The Mirror Line
activities.body:
Imagine a square with labelled corners A, B, C and D. You wonder how its mirror image would look. A vertical line can act as its line of symmetry. Reflection sends one side of that line to the other.

When you reflect across the vertical line, B and C move to the left side. The reflected points occupy the earlier positions of A and D. Also, A moves to B's position, and D moves to C's position.

Picture paper with a line of symmetry down the middle. A few drops of ink or paint go onto one half. You fold the paper and press the halves together. The two halves overlap completely. You open the paper and see matching marks on both halves.

You can use folding and cutting to make symmetrical shapes. Try cutting folded paper so the opened sheet has matching halves. If your design has a line of symmetry, it has reflection symmetry.

Punch holes through folded paper. When you open it, the holes form a symmetrical pattern. Each hole matches another hole across the fold.

lessons.title: Rotational Symmetry

activities.prompt: How can a shape look unchanged without folding perfectly onto itself?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Turning the Windmill
activities.body:
You meet a paper windmill. It looks symmetrical, yet it has no line of symmetry. Try folding its two halves. They do not exactly overlap, so the fold test fails.

Turn the windmill through 90° about its centre. It looks exactly the same. This shows that the windmill has rotational symmetry.

Rotational symmetry always has a fixed point about which the object turns. This fixed point is called the centre of rotation. Try a turn smaller than 90°. The windmill does not look the same.

An angle of symmetry makes a figure look exactly the same after rotation. The windmill has symmetry angles of 90° and 180°. It also has symmetry angles of 270° and 360°. A 360° angle is always an angle of symmetry.

A square gives another example. It overlaps with itself after a 90° rotation. Compare folding with turning. The windmill passes the turning test, but not the folding test.

activities.title: What is rotational symmetry?
activities.body: Rotational symmetry means a shape looks the same after it turns. It turns around one point that does not move. This point is the centre of rotation. The paper windmill has rotational symmetry. When it turns 90° about its centre, it looks the same. Its symmetry angles are 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°. It has no line of symmetry.

This point is the centre of rotation.
The windmill has symmetry angles of 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°.

activities.title: Rotating Radial-Arm Figures
activities.body:
You begin with a radial-arm figure on two pieces of paper. Cut it out carefully.

You explore the four-arm figure first. The adjacent central dotted lines are 90° apart. Then try changing it so it has only two symmetry angles.

You rotate your cutout. This helps you check whether the figure has rotational symmetry. Watch the arms and compare their positions.

You now meet an unequal three-arm figure. It has no rotational symmetry. To make a three-arm design overlap, angle A must overlap angle B.

You next explore a symmetrical three-arm design. All three angles must be equal. The angle between adjacent arms is 120°. For five arms, the symmetry angles are 72°, 144°, 216°, 288° and 360°. For six arms, they are 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300° and 360°. Each angle is a multiple of the smallest angle.

activities.title: Checking Rotational Symmetry
activities.body: Rotational symmetry means the shape looks the same after a turn. Turning a cutout helps you check this. A four-arm figure has dotted lines from its middle. Next dotted lines are 90° apart. A symmetrical three-arm design has 120° between arms next to each other. A three-arm figure with unequal arms has no rotational symmetry. A five-arm design has angles: 72°, 144°, 216°, 288° and 360°. A six-arm design has angles: 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300° and 360°. Symmetry angles are multiples (times-table numbers) of the smallest angle.
keyPoints: Turning a cutout helps check rotational symmetry.
In a symmetrical design, arms next to each other have equal angles.
Symmetry angles are multiples (times-table numbers) of the smallest angle.

lessons.title: Symmetry of Circles and the Whole Chapter

activities.prompt: What makes a circle seem unchanged, even when it spins?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Circle Symmetry Tour
activities.body:
Imagine a circle waiting quietly. You turn it, and it looks exactly the same. Would you call this symmetry?

You can turn it through any angle, and it still matches itself. A circle therefore coincides with itself after any rotation. Every diameter is also a line of symmetry for the circle.

Now you meet fans, flowers and wheels. These objects show rotational symmetry. Some figures have several lines of symmetry. Others may have several angles of symmetry.

An angle of symmetry lies strictly between 0° and 360°. If a figure has such an angle, it has rotational symmetry. The point where you turn it is called the centre of rotation.

You see that some figures have a line of symmetry but no angle of symmetry. Other figures have angles of symmetry but no lines of symmetry. Then you find shapes with both lines and angles of symmetry. So, what makes a figure seem unchanged? You compare its lines, angles and centre of rotation.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Circles and Symmetry
activities.body: An angle of symmetry shows rotational symmetry. A circle matches itself after any turn. The centre is the point of rotation (the point you turn around). A diameter is a straight line through the centre. Every diameter is a line of symmetry. An angle of symmetry is more than 0° and less than 360°. A shape can have lines, angles, or both kinds of symmetry.
keyPoints: A circle matches itself after any turn.
Every diameter is a line of symmetry.
Symmetry can be lines, angles, or both.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.title: Order the Rotation Steps
activities.prompt: Put these steps for rotating a circle in order.
items: Choose an angle strictly between 0° and 360°.
Rotate the circle through the chosen angle.
activities.explanation: A circle matches itself after any rotation. The chosen angle must lie strictly between 0° and 360°.

activities.prompt: A circular wheel has 8 identical spokes spaced evenly around a 360-degree turn. Starting at one spoke, how many degrees does it turn to pass through 2 matching sectors?
activities.explanation: The 8 equal sectors share a 360-degree turn, so one sector is 45 degrees. Passing through 2 matching sectors means making 2 equal turns. 2 × 45 = 90 degrees.
steps: The 8 equal sectors share a 360-degree turn, so one sector is 45 degrees.
Passing through 2 matching sectors means making 2 equal turns.
2 × 45 = 90 degrees.
activities.hint: First find the angle of one sector, then count 2 sectors.

Passing through {k} matching sectors means making {k} equal turns.

activities.prompt: Explain why the rangoli has symmetry.
activities.answer: The red petals come back onto themselves after a 90˚ turn around the centre, and the other parts return in the same way. This shows that the rangoli’s parts repeat in a definite pattern. That arrangement is why the rangoli has symmetry.
points: Mentions the 90˚ turn around the centre.
Says that the red petals return onto themselves.
Says that the other parts return in the same way.
Connects the repeating pattern with symmetry.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A learner is checking paper-folding designs. Figure (a) is a blue triangle with a dotted line. When the learner folds along the dotted line, one half of the triangle covers the other half completely, so the two matching pieces are mirror halves. The learner then compares two puzzle-piece halves and sees that they are not mirror halves. Later, a square is folded vertically, horizontally, and diagonally, and each fold is identified as a line of symmetry.
activities.prompt: What should the learner conclude about the two puzzle-piece halves?
options: They should be folded along a line of symmetry.
They should be described as mirror halves.
They should be described as non-mirror halves.
They must exactly overlap when reflected.

why.They should be folded along a line of sy: Option A assumes that any two pieces come from a symmetry fold.
why.They should be described as mirror halve: Option B contradicts what the learner observed about the puzzle pieces.
why.They must exactly overlap when reflected: Option D wrongly assumes that the puzzle pieces exactly overlap.

activities.explanation: Option C is correct because the puzzle-piece halves are not mirror halves.

activities.context: A learner is checking paper-folding designs. Figure (a) is a blue triangle with a dotted line. When the learner folds along the dotted line, one half of the triangle covers the other half completely, so the two matching pieces are mirror halves. The learner then compares two puzzle-piece halves and sees that they are not mirror halves. Later, a square is folded vertically, horizontally, and diagonally, and each fold is identified as a line of symmetry.
activities.prompt: After folding the square vertically, horizontally, and diagonally, what should the learner record?
options: Only the vertical fold qualifies; the other folds do not.
The vertical and horizontal folds qualify, but the diagonal fold does not.
The vertical, horizontal, and diagonal folds all qualify.
None of these folds qualifies because the square is not made of matching halves.

why.Only the vertical fold qualifies; the ot: Option A wrongly excludes the horizontal and diagonal folds.
why.The vertical and horizontal folds qualif: Option B wrongly excludes the diagonal fold.
why.None of these folds qualifies because th: Option D wrongly claims that the square does not have matching halves.

activities.explanation: Option C correctly records every folding line shown to work.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the triangle's two matching halves and the two puzzle-piece halves?
activities.answer: The triangle's matching halves exactly overlap when it is folded along the dotted line, so they are mirror halves and the dotted line is a line of symmetry. The puzzle-piece halves are not mirror halves, so they do not match in that way.
points: The triangle's halves exactly overlap.
Mirror halves are matching halves.
The puzzle-piece halves are not mirror halves.
The dotted fold is a line of symmetry.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why the ink marks on the folded-and-opened paper have a matching pattern.
activities.answer: The paper is folded along a line of symmetry, so its two halves overlap completely. Reflection sends a point on one side of the line to the matching position on the other side. Therefore, the ink marks on one half have reflected copies on the other half.
points: The fold is along a line of symmetry.
The two halves overlap completely.
Reflection sends each point to the other side.
The ink marks have matching reflected positions.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During an art lesson, a student makes a paper windmill for a classroom display. The windmill looks symmetrical, but when she folds it, the two halves do not exactly overlap, so it has no line of symmetry. She then turns it 90° about its centre. It looks exactly the same, while a turn smaller than 90° does not make it look the same.
activities.prompt: The student turns the windmill a smaller amount than 90°. What should she expect to happen next?
options: The outline will no longer match the starting picture.
The outline will still match because any amount of turning works.
The outline will still match because a 90° turn works for every turn.
The outline will still match because 180° and 270° are also symmetry angles.

why.The outline will still match because any: This wrongly suggests that every angle is a symmetry angle.
why.The outline will still match because a 9: This confuses the known 90° symmetry angle with other angles.
why.The outline will still match because 180: This wrongly uses larger symmetry angles to justify a smaller turn.

activities.explanation: This is correct because a turn smaller than 90° does not preserve the windmill’s appearance.

activities.context: During an art lesson, a student makes a paper windmill for a classroom display. The windmill looks symmetrical, but when she folds it, the two halves do not exactly overlap, so it has no line of symmetry. She then turns it 90° about its centre. It looks exactly the same, while a turn smaller than 90° does not make it look the same.
activities.prompt: The student identifies the fixed point about which the windmill turns. Which name should she use for this point?
options: centre of rotation
centre of symmetry
centre of folding
centre of balance

why.centre of symmetry: This confuses rotational symmetry with the idea of symmetry as a whole.
why.centre of folding: This wrongly connects the fixed turning point with folding.
why.centre of balance: This describes a balance-related idea rather than the rotation’s fixed point.

activities.explanation: This is correct because the fixed point of a rotation is called the centre of rotation.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between line symmetry and rotational symmetry using the windmill.
activities.answer: Line symmetry is checked by folding a figure so its two halves overlap. Rotational symmetry is checked by turning the figure about a fixed point. This windmill has no line of symmetry, but a 90° turn about its centre makes it look exactly the same.
points: Line symmetry concerns matching two halves when folded.
Rotational symmetry involves turning about a fixed point.
The fixed point is the centre of rotation.
The windmill has rotational symmetry but no line of symmetry.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why the unequal three-arm design cannot overlap itself after a rotation.
activities.answer: The unequal three-arm design has arms of different sizes, so a turn cannot make the whole design match itself. For rotational symmetry, the rotated arms must all overlap in the same way. Since they do not, this unequal three-arm design has no rotational symmetry.
points: Rotation is used to check the whole design.
Unequal arms prevent a complete match.
The unequal design has no rotational symmetry.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

lessons.title: Integers and the Building of Fun

activities.prompt: How can a lift help you discover positive and negative numbers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Lift and the Number Ray
activities.body:
Welcome aboard. You begin beside a number ray that starts at zero. Zero comes before one and means nothing. You follow the ray to the right, and it continues for ever.

You enter the lift. It can move up or down between floors. Press the plus button twice, and you rise by two floors. Going down two floors is written as −2.

Now you explore the floors. The Food Court sits on Floor +1. The Toy Store lies on Floor −1. The plus sign shows a positive number, while the minus sign shows a negative number.

You meet zero again. It is neither positive nor negative. You stand at zero and remember that it means nothing.

Before you leave, you meet ten digits. Together, they can write numbers of any size in the Indian number system. Your journey ends, but the number ray keeps going right for ever.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Zero, signs, and moving floors
activities.body: Zero comes before 1 and means nothing. The number ray begins at 0 and continues right for ever. Ten digits can write numbers of any size in the Indian number system. Plus signs mark positive numbers, and minus signs mark negative numbers. Zero is neither positive nor negative. A lift moves up and down between floors. Going down two floors is written as – 2.
keyPoints: 0 represents nothing and comes before 1.
Positive numbers have plus signs; negative numbers have minus signs.
The lift moves between floors; down two floors is – 2.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you read signs and move between floors.

activities.prompt: What does 0 represent?
options: one floor
up two floors
nothing
down two floors
activities.explanation: Zero represents nothing. It comes before 1.

activities.prompt: The number ray continues to the left for ever.
activities.explanation: The number ray starts at 0. It continues to the right for ever.

activities.prompt: In the Indian number system, numbers of any size use _____ digits.
activities.hint: Write the number as a word.
activities.explanation: Ten digits can write numbers of any size in the Indian number system.

activities.prompt: Match each floor or sign to its meaning.
activities.explanation: The Food Court has a positive floor number. The Toy Store has a negative floor number.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order for a lift trip to the Toy Store.
items: Start at the Food Court on Floor + 1
Arrive at the Toy Store on Floor – 1
activities.explanation: The Food Court is on Floor +1. Going down two floors reaches the Toy Store on Floor –1.

activities.prompt: What happens if you press the plus button twice?
options: The lift moves down two floors
The lift moves up two floors
The lift moves to zero
The lift moves up one floor
activities.explanation: Pressing the plus button twice takes the lift up two floors.

activities.prompt: A lift leaves the Toy Store and moves up two floors. Where does it reach?
options: Floor 0
The Toy Store on Floor – 1
Floor + 2
The Food Court on Floor + 1
activities.explanation: The Toy Store is on Floor –1. Moving up two floors reaches Floor +1, where the Food Court is.

activities.prompt: A shop's number board has 4 places for writing a number. Each place can use any of the ten digits. How many digit choices are allowed in each place?
activities.explanation: There are ten digits available for each place.
activities.hint: Type the number.

lessons.title: Moving, Comparing and Finding Change

activities.prompt: Ready to discover what changes when a lift moves?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Lift Journey
activities.body:
You stand at the starting floor beside a lift. Its buttons invite you to explore movement. The starting floor plus the movement gives the target floor.

From Floor + 1, move by two floors. Moving from Floor + 1 by two floors reaches Floor + 3. Combining button presses is a form of addition. You can check the target by finding the movement needed.

Now try the reverse. The inverse of + 3 is – 3. Pressing the inverse of a floor number takes the lift back to zero. A positive movement and its inverse add to zero.

Compare nearby floors as you travel. Floor + 3 is lower than Floor + 4. Floor – 4 is lower than Floor – 3. Every negative number is less than zero. Every positive number is greater than zero.

Perhaps two quantities differ. Subtraction can mean making two unequal quantities equal. Find the starting floor, then find the target. The movement needed is the target floor minus the starting floor.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Lift Movements Work
activities.body: A lift’s starting floor and movement give its target floor. Moving up by three floors from Floor + 1 reaches Floor + 3. Combining button presses is addition. An inverse movement undoes another movement. The inverse of + 3 is – 3. A positive movement and its inverse make zero. You can compare floors and find the needed movement.
keyPoints: Add the movement to the starting floor.
The inverse of + 3 is – 3.
A movement and its inverse make zero.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you move, compare and undo lift movements.

activities.title: Jump along the number line

tasks.say: Start at 1 and add -5.
tasks.then: You cross zero and land on -4.

tasks.say: Start at -4 and add 4.
tasks.then: A number and its opposite make zero.

activities.takeaway: Adding a negative moves left, adding a positive moves right.
activities.explanation: Adding a negative moves left, adding a positive moves right.

activities.title: Choose the Target Floor
activities.prompt: You start on Floor + 1. Moving up two floors reaches which floor?
options: Floor + 2
Floor + 3
Floor + 4
Floor – 3
activities.explanation: Floor + 1 plus two floors reaches Floor + 3.

activities.title: Find the Inverse
activities.prompt: The inverse of + 3 is – ______.
activities.hint: Use the opposite movement.
activities.explanation: The inverse of + 3 is – 3. These movements make zero together.

activities.title: Match Each Idea
activities.prompt: Match each left-hand idea with its correct meaning.
activities.explanation: Inverse movements undo each other, and the facts compare floors and numbers.

activities.prompt: A lift starts at Floor 5 and must reach Floor 8. What upward movement is needed, in floors?
activities.explanation: Subtract the starting floor number from the target floor number: target - start. For example, 7 - 2 = 5 floors.
activities.hint: Type the number.

activities.prompt: A lift is at Floor 7 + 1. It moves up 2 floors. What floor number does it reach?
activities.explanation: Add the starting floor number and the upward movement: f + 1 + 2. The lift reaches Floor 7 + 3.

activities.prompt: A lift goes up 6 floors. Then it goes up 3 more floors. How many floors does it go up in all?
activities.explanation: Combining the two button presses is addition: a + b. The total upward movement is 9 floors.
activities.hint: Type the number.

activities.prompt: A lift is at Floor 2 + 3. The down button moves it down 3 floors. What floor number does it reach?
activities.explanation: The inverse of + 3 is - 3, so add 3 and then subtract 3: f + 3 - 3. The lift reaches Floor 2.
activities.hint: Type the number.

activities.title: Plan a Lift Journey
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the right order. Use them to plan a lift trip.
items: Find the target floor (where you want to go)
Subtract the starting floor from the target floor
activities.explanation: The needed movement is the target floor minus the starting floor. Add the movement to the starting floor to reach the target.

activities.prompt: One lift is 3 floors up from Floor 0. Another lift is 2 floors down from Floor 0. How many floors apart are they?
activities.explanation: The floor numbers are a and 0 - b. Their distance is a - (0 - b). That is a + b floors.

activities.prompt: Which floor number is lower, Floor 7 + 3 or Floor 7 - 4?
activities.explanation: A floor below Floor 7 is lower than one above Floor 7. Therefore, Floor 7 - 4 is lower.

lessons.title: Number Lines and Large Integers

activities.prompt: How can a small minus sign help you move on a big number line?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Large Numbers
activities.body:
You begin your tour at zero. Negative numbers lie to the left of zero. Moving right is positive movement.

Smaller numbers stay left of larger numbers. Start at 5 and move four steps to 9. You have added 4. Turn back from 9 to 3. That journey moves – 6 steps. From 3 to – 2, you move – 5 steps.

Now imagine subtracting a negative number. This works like adding the corresponding positive number. The operation becomes addition of the matching positive number.

Next, compare + 2000 and – 200. Their difference is + 2200. You find it by adding the corresponding positive number, 200.

Finally, remember that subtraction can always become addition. Use the inverse of the number being subtracted. Positive numbers usually leave out the plus sign. Your number-line tour now has a simple rule.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Reading and Moving on a Number Line
activities.body: A number line helps you see numbers. Negative numbers are to the left of zero. Smaller numbers are to the left of bigger numbers. Moving right means the positive direction. Moving from 5 to 9 adds 4. Moving from 9 to 3 means a move of –6 steps. Subtracting a negative number works like adding a positive number. You can also change a subtraction into an addition. This uses an inverse (the opposite action).
keyPoints: Negative numbers are to the left of zero.
Moving right means the positive direction.
Subtracting a negative number works like adding a positive number.
activities.explanation: Number lines make big numbers and negative moves easier to see.

activities.title: Jump along the number line

tasks.say: Start at 1 and add -5.
tasks.then: You cross zero and land on -4.

tasks.say: Start at -4 and add 4.
tasks.then: A number and its opposite make zero.

activities.takeaway: Adding a negative moves left, adding a positive moves right.
activities.explanation: Adding a negative moves left, adding a positive moves right.

activities.title: Where Negative Numbers Lie
activities.prompt: On a number line, where do negative numbers lie?
options: To the left of zero
To the right of zero
Above zero
Below zero
activities.explanation: Negative numbers lie to the left of zero.

activities.title: Writing Positive Numbers
activities.prompt: We usually leave out the plus sign when we write positive numbers.
activities.explanation: Yes. We usually write positive numbers without a plus sign.

activities.title: Finding a Difference
activities.prompt: The difference between + 2000 and – 200 is + ______.
activities.hint: Add 2000 and 200.
activities.explanation: The difference between + 2000 and – 200 is + 2200.

activities.title: Match Each Movement
activities.prompt: Match each movement with the correct change.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows the change in direction and size.

activities.title: Moving Right
activities.prompt: Moving to the right means moving in the negative direction.
activities.explanation: Moving to the right means moving in the positive direction.

activities.title: Moving Across Zero
activities.prompt: What movement takes you from 3 to – 2?
options: – 5 steps
+ 5 steps
– 2 steps
+ 2 steps
activities.explanation: Moving from 3 to – 2 means moving – 5 steps.

activities.title: Order Numbers on a Number Line
activities.prompt: Put these numbers in order from left to right on a number line.
activities.explanation: Negative numbers come before positive numbers. Smaller numbers come first.

lessons.title: The Token Model

activities.prompt: What happens when positive and negative tokens meet?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Token Model
activities.body:
You begin on Floor 0. The lift attendant is there with an empty pocket. This is your starting point.

You see green positive tokens and red negative tokens. You press the plus button, and you take a positive token. You press the minus button, and you take a negative token.

Now you meet five positive tokens and three negative tokens together. Their value is + 2. You discover that one positive token and one negative token cancel each other. Together, they make a zero pair.

You remove all zero pairs from the five positive and three negative tokens. Two positive tokens remain. The token model shows that subtraction can work through tokens too.

Try adding + 5 and – 8. Your sum is – 3. Then find the difference between – 7 and – 5. The difference is – 2. You now see how tokens can represent positive and negative values.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Positive, Negative and Zero Pairs
activities.body: The lift attendant uses two kinds of tokens. Green tokens are positive. Red tokens are negative. Pressing the plus button means taking a positive token. Pressing the minus button means taking a negative token. A positive token and a negative token cancel each other. Together, they make a zero pair. Removing zero pairs shows the final value.
keyPoints: Green tokens are positive.
Red tokens are negative.
A positive and negative token make a zero pair.
activities.explanation: This model shows how positive and negative tokens work together.

activities.prompt: Which token is positive?
options: The green token
The red token
The empty pocket
activities.explanation: Green tokens are positive, while red tokens are negative.

activities.prompt: A lift attendant starts with an empty pocket. The attendant presses the plus button 2 times. What is the value in token units?
activities.explanation: Each press of the plus button adds one positive token. So 2 positive tokens have a value of 2 token units.
activities.hint: Type the number.

activities.prompt: The lift worker presses the plus button 4 times. The lift worker presses the minus button 1 time. What is the total pocket value, in token units?
activities.explanation: The positive tokens add 4. The negative tokens subtract 1. So the total is 4 - 1 token units.

activities.prompt: The pocket has 6 positive tokens and 5 negative tokens. After removing all zero pairs, how many positive tokens remain?
activities.explanation: Each negative token cancels one positive token. After removing the zero pairs, 6 - 5 positive tokens remain.
activities.hint: Type the number.

activities.prompt: Match each token situation to its result.
pairs: Five positive and three negative tokens
One positive token and one negative token
Five positive and three negative tokens, with zero pairs removed
activities.explanation: A zero pair cancels, so only two positive tokens remain.

activities.prompt: Put the token steps in order.
items: Five positive and three negative tokens
activities.explanation: Removing zero pairs leaves two positive tokens and a value of + 2.

activities.prompt: What is the sum of + 5 and – 8?
activities.explanation: The sum of + 5 and – 8 is – 3.

activities.prompt: A marble tray has 10 marbles. The lift attendant uses 3 negative tokens to take marbles away, one marble for each token. How many marbles remain?
activities.explanation: Taking away 3 marbles from 10 marbles leaves 10 - 3 marbles.
activities.hint: Type the number.

lessons.title: Integers in Banking, Heights and Temperature

activities.prompt: How can one number show money, height and temperature?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Banking, Heights and Temperature
activities.body:
You begin at the bank and open your passbook. A credit appears when money is added. A debit appears when money is taken out.

Next, you imagine that some banks allow an account balance to become negative temporarily. A bank may charge interest or a fee when the balance is negative. It is generally better to try to keep a positive bank balance.

Now you change your viewpoint. Credits can be treated as positive numbers, while debits can be treated as negative numbers.

After that, you explore the idea of sea level. The height at sea level is 0 metres. Heights above sea level are represented by positive numbers. Heights below sea level are represented by negative numbers.

Finally, you visit a thermometer. Celsius is the unit used for measuring temperature. You see that 0°C indicates the freezing point of water.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Understanding Positive and Negative Numbers
activities.body: In a bank passbook (a book that shows your money), a credit means money added. A debit means money taken out. Credits can be positive. Debits can be negative. Some banks let a balance go negative. Then the bank may charge interest or a fee. For heights, sea level is 0 metres. Above sea level is positive. Below sea level is negative. Temperature is measured in Celsius. At 0°C, water is at its freezing point.
keyPoints: Credits can be positive, and debits can be negative.
Heights above sea level are positive, and below are negative.
Celsius is the unit for measuring temperature.
activities.explanation: These signs help you read bank money, heights and temperature.

tasks.say: Start at 1 and add -5.
tasks.then: You cross zero and land on -4.

tasks.say: Start at -4 and add 4.
tasks.then: A number and its opposite make zero.

activities.takeaway: Adding a negative moves left, adding a positive moves right.
activities.explanation: Adding a negative moves left, adding a positive moves right.

activities.title: What does a credit show?
activities.prompt: A credit in a bank book shows that money was:
options: taken out
added
measured
charged
activities.explanation: A credit shows that money was added to a bank account.

activities.title: Debits and money
activities.prompt: A bank passbook shows a debit when money is taken out.
activities.explanation: A debit shows money leaving the bank account.

activities.prompt: A bank passbook shows a credit of 100 rupees. What is the signed credit amount in rupees?
activities.explanation: A credit is positive, so the signed amount is 100 rupees.
activities.hint: Type the number.

activities.prompt: An account has 750 rupees and receives a credit of 500 rupees. What is the new balance in rupees?
activities.explanation: Adding the credit gives 750+500 rupees.
activities.hint: Type the number.

activities.prompt: An account has 1500 rupees and a debit of 100 rupees is made. What is the new balance in rupees?
activities.explanation: Subtracting the debit gives 1500-100 rupees.
activities.hint: Type the number.

activities.prompt: An account has a credit of 700 rupees and a debit of 200 rupees. The credit is larger than the debit. What is the signed balance in rupees that the customer should try to keep?
activities.explanation: The signed balance is 700-200 rupees. It is positive, so it is better to try to keep it.

activities.title: Order the heights
activities.prompt: Put these heights in order from lowest to highest.
activities.explanation: Below sea level is negative, sea level is 0 metres, and above sea level is positive.

activities.prompt: Sea level is 0 metres. Place A is 30 metres below sea level. Place B is 60 metres above sea level. How many metres is the difference in height between A and B?
activities.explanation: Place A has height -30 metres. To find the difference, subtract A's height from B's height. That gives 60 - (-30) = 60 + 30 metres.
